idiom_name: T? (Nullable<T> for value types, nullable reference types for references) plus the Try pattern
implementation_notes: Absence is part of the type system in two complementary ways. For value types, T? is System.Nullable<T> with HasValue/Value, an unset T? is the default value of the type, and boxing an empty T? produces a null reference. For reference types, nullable reference types make string? versus string a compile-time contract checked by null-state flow analysis, with attributes such as [NotNullWhen(true)] describing richer API contracts; Microsoft documents this as static analysis that minimizes NullReferenceException, with runtime behaviour unchanged. The library convention that carries absence out of a method is the Try pattern (bool TryGetValue(TKey key, out TValue value)) together with [NotNullWhen(true)], used throughout the BCL. The classic Maybe wrapper is replaced by these two mechanisms plus the Try convention; a hand-written Option<T> struct is the fallback only when nesting must be observable, because Nullable<T> cannot be a reference type and cannot nest.
pitfalls: For reference types the annotation is compile-time only: the runtime type is unchanged, reflection and serializers still see a plain string, and a ! or a cast silences the analysis without changing behaviour.
Nullable<T> boxes to a plain T or to a null reference, so passing it through object or an interface erases the has-a-value distinction.
Nullable<T> cannot nest and cannot be a reference type: when outer and inner absence must be distinguishable, the annotations cannot express it.

default(SomeStruct) leaves non-nullable reference fields holding null without a warning, and a new array of references starts all-null, so 'non-nullable' is a promise the compiler only partially checks.

variants.name: Hand-written Option<T> struct
variants.idiom_name: readonly struct Option<T> with Some/None and Match/Map/GetOrElse
variants.implementation_notes: A readonly struct Option<T> with an implicit conversion from T, default(Option<T>) as None, and Match/Map/GetOrElse surface gives what Nullable<T> cannot: nesting (Option<Option<T>>), use with reference types without giving null a second meaning, and a monadic API that composes chains of partial steps. Choose it in code bases that already speak Option/Result, or where a nullable column must be told apart from a stored null. It is not the platform default: it needs its own equality, hashing and serialization story, and it duplicates what the BCL provides for the simple cases.
pitfalls: default(Option<T>) must mean None, so a constructor that takes T must reject null or the type silently promotes a null to Some.
Equality, hashing and serialization must be defined deliberately (value equality for T, None as a single state) or dictionary keys and JSON behave surprisingly.
A struct wrapper over a reference type has the same null hole as string?: the invariant only holds if the constructors are the only entry point.
